video_title: The Return of Economic Populism and the End of Two Percent | Vincent Deluard
gist: Vincent Deluard reads the US midterms as an anti-war, anti-elite economic-populist wave and argues that secular inflation, fiscal dominance and the end of the 2% target are the real regime. He ties this to a reversing super peso and yen carry, Canada's capital-repatriation leverage, and a French debt and political crisis (first hour only; the rest is paywalled).

insights.claim: The midterm result is a once-in-a-century-scale rejection of Trump and MAGA, and Deluard expects the movement to gather strength into 2028.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Expect continued Democratic momentum and policy gridlock through 2028 rather than a one-off swing.
insights.quote: a profound rejection I think of of Trump and and MAGA

insights.claim: Campaign spending decoupled from outcomes: Elon Musk's heavy Texas spending was wasted, suggesting the 20-year link between fundraising and winning has been severed.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Money-driven political forecasting and donor-class influence models deserve less weight.

insights.claim: The election was fought on prices and corruption, not culture-war issues, signalling a return to class-warfare politics and a rise of left-wing populism, the mirror image of the Tea Party.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Policy risk skews toward redistribution, affordability and anti-elite measures.
insights.quote: we are getting back to kind of a class warfare environment

insights.claim: Americans have repeatedly elected the least pro-war candidate since 2000; Trump's Iran war, and the inflation and high gasoline prices it brought, betrayed his core mandate.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: War-driven energy price shocks are a political liability that compounds affordability stress.
insights.quote: the American electorate just really doesn't want to be involved in wars anymore

themes.theme: Secular inflation and the end of the 2% target

insights.claim: Structurally high deficits and fiscal dominance make the 2% inflation target a fading fiction; the US has missed it for six years and a task force is reviewing how inflation is computed.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Position for higher-for-longer inflation and for fiscal winning the monetary-versus-fiscal fight.
insights.quote: it's it's really only a matter of time

insights.claim: Fiscal-versus-monetary conflict is global (US, Brazil, Europe), and Deluard expects fiscal to win in every major democracy.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Central-bank independence is the asset to short in portfolio construction.
insights.quote: I think the outcome will be that fiscal will win.

insights.claim: Subscriptions, services and intangibles break the link between consumption and payment, cause annual price resets that distort seasonal adjustment (January-February CPI surprises), and leave less discretionary spending to cut when gasoline spikes.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Watch early-year CPI prints and consumer stress in prepaid-heavy household budgets.

insights.claim: Personalized, algorithmic pricing erodes the 'representative consumer' behind CPI-U and shifts surplus from consumers to producers, which helps explain why inflation feels worse than the measured numbers.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Pricing power accrues to firms with customer data, and measured inflation understates felt inflation.
insights.quote: the consumer surplus gets taken over by the producer surplus

themes.theme: Super peso reversal and the end of the yen carry

insights.claim: The super peso (near 16 per dollar) was driven by strong US growth, USMCA nearshoring, remittances, digital nomads, tourism and a high carry funded partly in yen; all of these are now reversing at once.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Peso weakness is multi-causal, so a bounce is unlikely without several drivers turning.

insights.claim: Mexico's weak negotiating hand in the USMCA review, tariffs that target its role as a backdoor for Chinese goods, falling Cancun bookings (down 50-70% per Deluard) and a Banxico cut bias against a hiking Fed erode the carry.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Carry in MXN is losing support from rate differentials.

insights.claim: Deluard recommended clients trade the peso against the Canadian dollar, expecting the earlier trend (strong MXN, weak CAD) to invert.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Short MXN versus CAD is the expressed relative-value trade.
insights.quote: I would go with the peso of the north, the Canadian dollars.

insights.claim: The Japanese yen carry trade is ending and has been a major driver of asset prices, including the US tech/AI trade and the peso.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: BoJ tightening is a cross-asset risk, not just a yen story.
insights.quote: this Japanese carry trade and I'm sure we'll talk about it later is is is is over

insights.claim: The midterms do little to constrain tariffs, which run on executive orders, and may make them more likely as Trump's remaining lever; after the Supreme Court struck down emergency tariffs (about $200B refunded) and a roughly $300B deficit gap, tariffs are the only fast revenue source.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Expect tariff policy to re-emerge as a revenue tool, with trade-sensitive assets exposed.
insights.quote: Trump is like a toddler, right? I mean if he has a if he has a hammer

insights.claim: Canada's terms of trade (energy, fertilizer), pragmatic Carney leadership and rally-round-the-flag politics argue for a Canadian dollar turnaround after a decade of per-capita stagnation.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: CAD is a candidate for trend reversal against MXN.

insights.claim: Canadian pensions (over $3T, about 65% in the US) give Canada leverage in USMCA talks because the US needs foreign capital to fund its deficit, so repatriation is a credible threat.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Capital-account threats matter more than trade-share arguments in negotiations.
insights.quote: on the capital side the opposite is true

insights.claim: Foreign inflows funding the US trade deficit (about 3-4% of GDP) drove a decade of US outperformance; national capitalism, with Japan, Europe and Canada pulling savings home for grids, energy and defense, is one of the biggest risks to US valuations.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: US asset valuations carry a repatriation risk that is poorly priced.
insights.quote: I would think it's it's one of the biggest risks.

themes.theme: France: debt crisis and populist polarization

insights.claim: France ticks the debt-crisis boxes: debt about 120% of GDP, deficit of 5-6%, over half held abroad (much by Japan), no national currency to print, and a serious political crisis.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: French debt is the euro-area contagion channel to watch.
insights.quote: France really ticks all all the boxes of a of a debt crisis

insights.claim: The French and German establishments ostracized extremes, hollowing out the centre to 15-20%; April's runoff is likely far-left versus far-right and Le Pen, polling near 40%, will probably win.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Political risk premium on OATs likely persists whichever extreme wins.
insights.quote: eventually she will win the election

insights.claim: Even Le Pen's win is not benign for French bonds: unlike Meloni, her party lacks coalition culture and governing experience, and her economic instincts (lower pension age, bigger state) lean left.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard
insights.so_what: Do not assume a 'populist moderates in office' relief rally in French debt.
